questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A lede that opens on scene instead of news
questions.learningObjective: identify what a report's opening line places before the reader

stimulus.body: The lane outside the depot was still cordoned off on Thursday evening, a shipping container standing across the entrance and a notice taped to the railings. In 2019 the yard had no gates at all. The company said on Friday that the fence was raised the following winter, after goods worth 40,000 pounds were taken from the yard.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report begins: 'The lane outside the depot was still cordoned off on Thursday evening, a shipping container standing across the entrance and a notice taped to the railings. In 2019 the yard had no gates at all. The company said on Friday that the fence was raised the following winter, after goods worth 40,000 pounds were taken from the yard.' What does this opening do to a reader who meets only the first line?

options.text: Hold the news back, since the first two lines carry scene and the theft arrives only in the third
Give the reader a place to picture, which is the work an opening paragraph exists to do
options.misconception: treats atmosphere as the job of a lede, when a lede's job is to name the event

options.text: Warn that the report concerns a fence, so the reader is ready for the third line
options.misconception: reads the third line's subject as the report's subject, when the report's subject is the theft

options.text: Fix the time of writing, since a day and an evening appear in the first line
options.misconception: takes a scene's clock as the report's clock, when the report's own date sits in the third line

questions.explanation: A lede is written for a reader who may never reach the second paragraph, so it must carry the event itself, not the weather around it. Here the first line gives cordons, a container and a notice, and the second gives a state of affairs in 2019, and only the third sentence says that goods were taken and that a fence followed. Two of the report's three opening lines are therefore doing work that belongs further down, and a reader who scans has spent the whole of their attention on the least consequential part of the story. Atmosphere is not forbidden in a news report; it is simply worth what a lede is worth, which is that a reader can act on the first line or move on. Nothing here is false, and the sequence is the fault: the report has put its scene where its news ought to be.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence tells a reader what happened.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Passive agency in a crime lead
questions.learningObjective: name the actor a passive lead has removed

stimulus.body: A man was arrested in the early hours of Tuesday at a warehouse in the eastern dock area and is expected to appear before magistrates on Wednesday, police said. Detectives recovered 300 kilos of uncut tobacco from a container that had been standing in the yard since November. No charges have been filed and no officer was named.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report reads: 'A man was arrested in the early hours of Tuesday at a warehouse in the eastern dock area and is expected to appear before magistrates on Wednesday, police said. Detectives recovered 300 kilos of uncut tobacco from a container that had been standing in the yard since November. No charges have been filed and no officer was named.' What does this lead leave a reader without?

options.text: Any sign the tobacco was moving, since the container is said to have stood in the yard since November
options.misconception: reads 'standing' as 'waiting to be shipped', importing a claim the sentence does not make

options.text: An agent for the arrest, since the sentence makes the arrest an event and names nobody doing it
Evidence that the man's name has been withheld, since no name appears at any point in the report
options.misconception: supposes a suppression where the report identifies no one, which is ordinary before a charge

options.text: A reason to link the yard to the arrest site, since both places appear in the same paragraph
options.misconception: ties two separate locations together, when the arrest is at a warehouse and the container is in a yard

questions.explanation: Read the first clause as a description of what happened to the man rather than as a description of what anyone did. The subject of the sentence is a man, the verb is was arrested, and the agent that English would normally name, the arresting officers, is absent; the only person to whom an action is later attributed in the paragraph is police, and that word attaches to said, not to the arrest. A reader of a crime lead needs to know who acted, because the acting body is what distinguishes a routine arrest from a raid, a stop on suspicion from an arrest after a warrant, and a warrantless arrest from one made in consequence of a search. The report's second sentence, which gives Detectives as the subject of recovered, shows the writer can name an agent when the shape of the sentence allows it, and the first sentence's shape does not. The other three readings each import something the words do not support: a claim about the container's purpose, a suppression the report never claims, and a connection between two locations the paragraph keeps apart.
questions.hint: Find the sentence that says who arrested him.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A nut paragraph that repeats the lede
questions.learningObjective: judge what a nut paragraph is for after reading one that adds nothing

stimulus.body: The harbour road will close for six weeks from 14 April while a culvert is replaced beneath it. The harbour road will close for six weeks from 14 April. Local buses will use a diverted route through Marsh Lane, and the diversion for cars is signed from the junction at Kiln Street.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report reads: 'The harbour road will close for six weeks from 14 April while a culvert is replaced beneath it. The harbour road will close for six weeks from 14 April. Local buses will use a diverted route through Marsh Lane, and the diversion for cars is signed from the junction at Kiln Street.' What has the second sentence done?

options.text: Set the most important fact in its own short sentence, which is a standard form in reports
options.misconception: misses that the shorter sentence carries less, not more, because it drops the work and the reason

options.text: Separated the news from its explanation, giving the reader the event before the detail
options.misconception: invents a division; both sentences carry the event and neither carries explanation

options.text: Repeated the first sentence without adding the reason or the consequence
Marked the start of the background, so a reader can see where the news ends
options.misconception: finds a shift of level where the second sentence is a subset of the first

questions.explanation: The second sentence is the first sentence with the work and the reason removed. What the first says is that the road closes, that it closes for six weeks, that it closes from 14 April, and that a culvert is being replaced there. What the second says is that the road closes, that it closes for six weeks, and that it closes from 14 April. The one phrase the repetition loses is while a culvert is replaced beneath it, which is the only thing in the pair that tells a reader why. A nut paragraph is the part of a report that says why the event matters, what is at stake and what happens next, and it earns its place by carrying weight the lede cannot; a second copy of the lede carries none. Neither of the two sentences names a consequence, so a reader who wanted to know what the closure costs them has to wait for the third, which is the only sentence in the paragraph that adds a fact at all.
questions.hint: Compare the two sentences word for word and see what the shorter one has lost.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A story with no nut paragraph
questions.learningObjective: diagnose what a report is missing when it never says why the event matters
questions.practice: structure audit of a short report

stimulus.body: A fire at a warehouse on Tannery Street destroyed 400 square metres of stock on Sunday night, the fire service said. The service said the blaze started at about 02:00 in a loading bay and that two crews brought it under by 04:30. No one was hurt. The owner of the building, a firm that leases units on the estate, could not be reached.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report runs: 'A fire at a warehouse on Tannery Street destroyed 400 square metres of stock on Sunday night, the fire service said. The service said the blaze started at about 02:00 in a loading bay and that two crews brought it under by 04:30. No one was hurt. The owner of the building, a firm that leases units on the estate, could not be reached.' What does this report never do?

options.text: Give the time the fire started, which the second sentence supplies
options.misconception: misses a fact the second sentence does supply, about 02:00

options.text: Attribute each claim to a source, which every sentence here already does
options.misconception: misses that two sentences carry a named source and the rest carry none

options.text: Name the person who owns the building, which the fourth sentence says it could not do
options.misconception: misses that the report states the owner could not be reached, which is a different thing from naming

options.text: Say what the loss means for the people who worked or traded there

questions.explanation: Every sentence in the report is about the fire itself: where it was, how big it was, when it began, when it was put out, that nobody was hurt, and that the owner could not be reached. Not one of them is about what the fire means. A report that stops there leaves a reader with a fact and no reason to read the next one, and it is this sentence, not the lede, that a report on a commercial estate exists to supply: how many businesses were affected, whether anyone has lost trading, whether the unit will be rebuilt and by whom. Note also what the fourth sentence does and does not do. Saying the owner could not be reached is a statement about the reporting, not a statement about the loss, and it is the last thing in the report rather than a way into it. The three alternatives are all things the report has in fact done, which is what makes them wrong: the time, the sourcing and the acknowledged absence of an owner are each present in the text, and only the consequence is not.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader is left holding that would make them want a second paragraph.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The background tail of an inverted pyramid
questions.learningObjective: explain why the least load-bearing material goes last in a hard-news report
questions.stem: A hard-news report is built so that its most important material comes first and its least important comes last. Why is it written that way?

options.text: Because the report may be cut at any length, and a cut from the bottom keeps the story whole
Because readers finish the first paragraph and skip the rest, so the end must hold the worst news
options.misconception: puts the worst news at the end, which is the one place a reader is most likely to abandon the report

options.text: Because a report is checked by a sub-editor who removes whatever repeats, so repetition must sit late
options.misconception: ties the shape to sub-editing rather than to how far a reader is likely to get

options.text: Because the background of a story is the part most likely to be found wrong, so it is placed where errors cost least
options.misconception: reasons about error-checking, when the ordering answers a question about readers, not editors

questions.explanation: The shape exists because a report is consumed under conditions its writer does not control. It may be truncated by a length limit, by a headline slot, by a broadcast bulletin, or by a reader who simply closes the tab, and the most frequent truncation is from the bottom. If the ordering is right, a cut at any point leaves a report that still says what happened, to whom, where, and what follows, because the answer to those questions is at the top. If the ordering is wrong, the same cut can leave a report that opens on a charity's founding meeting and never mentions the fire. That is also why the most consequential material belongs high: consequence is what makes a reader continue, so a report that ends on consequence has put its least useful material in the position where it is most likely to be read. The other three answers each attach the ordering to something other than the reader's likely stopping point, and none of them explains what a cut leaves behind.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a report must be shortened.

questions.topic: A background paragraph that reads as new
questions.learningObjective: spot a recycled paragraph that a reader cannot tell is background

stimulus.body: The council has said it will publish a list of the sites cleared for redevelopment by the end of the month. A list of the sites cleared for redevelopment was published in March and again last July, and the council said at the time that it would review the list every year. Two of the sites on the new list are among the eleven published in July.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report reads: 'The council has said it will publish a list of the sites cleared for redevelopment by the end of the month. A list of the sites cleared for redevelopment was published in March and again last July, and the council said at the time that it would review the list every year. Two of the sites on the new list are among the eleven published in July.' What has the second paragraph failed to mark?

options.text: Which body will publish the list, since the first sentence says only that a list will be published
options.misconception: misses that the council is named as the publisher in the first sentence

options.text: That its material has appeared before, so a reader cannot tell what is new in this report
How many sites the list will contain, since the report mentions eleven earlier ones
options.misconception: supplies a number nobody needs, when the report is about novelty not size

options.text: Why the council waited, since a reader will want a reason for the delay
options.misconception: asks for motive that a report may reasonably leave until it has the material

questions.explanation: The second paragraph is background and it is written so that a reader cannot tell. It contains a list of the sites cleared for redevelopment, a claim that this was published in March and last July, and a commitment to review the list every year, but no date, no past tense marking it as prior, and nothing to tell the reader that this material is not new. Inverted-pyramid ordering assumes that a report's readers will treat its second paragraph as more or less current, and this paragraph quietly spends the reader's attention on material that has been published twice before. The fact that the paragraph's own content is interesting, and that it ends with the genuinely new comparison, does not repair the failure, because the reader has had to work out the newness themselves. Each of the three alternatives asks for something the report either supplies in its first sentence or is under no obligation to supply at all.
questions.hint: Ask which sentences in this report are reporting something the council has said before.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Attribution to a role instead of a speaker
questions.learningObjective: judge when a role can stand in for a named speaker in a report
questions.stem: A report quotes 'a council officer' where a named official was available and had agreed to be named. What is the effect of the substitution?

options.text: The report becomes shorter, since a role needs fewer words than a name and a title
options.misconception: measures the effect in characters, when the reader's ability to judge the source is what changes

options.text: The quote is protected from being withdrawn, since a role cannot be sued for a remark
options.misconception: invents a legal effect, where a named official can withdraw a remark from a role the same way

options.text: A reader cannot weigh what was said against what that person is entitled to say
The reader is spared a title the report would otherwise have to explain
options.misconception: supplies a courtesy the report owes no reader, and the omission is not about politeness

questions.explanation: Attribution does two jobs at once. It tells a reader who spoke, which establishes that somebody said it, and it tells a reader what standing the speaker has, which tells the reader how much weight the words can carry. A named official with a portfolio is a checkable thing: a reader can weigh a statement about a budget against the office that holds the budget. A council officer is a category, and any statement in the world can be made to fit inside it, so the reader is left holding words with no scale attached. That matters most where the words are doing work the reader must check, which is why a report about a disputed figure is weakened more by an unnamed speaker than a report about a ceremony. The other three answers treat the substitution as a matter of economy, of legal protection or of politeness, and each of those is a real concern in newsrooms without being the effect on this reader.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do with the words that is no longer possible.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A quote attributed to a document rather than a person
questions.learningObjective: distinguish quoting a text from quoting the person who wrote it
questions.stem: A report says: 'The report states that the scheme will serve 340 households, the committee was told.' What has the sentence left the reader unable to do?

options.text: Judge the figure, since a number written in a report can be read by anyone
options.misconception: confuses availability with authority, when a number anyone can read is not a number anyone can test

options.text: Find the report, since a report can be asked for by name from the committee
options.misconception: supplies a route the sentence does not need, because the fault is the missing teller not the missing title

options.text: Tell whether the committee believed the figure, since being told is not the same as agreeing
options.misconception: reads agreement into a passive, when the question is who did the telling

options.text: Ask who told the committee, since the report and the telling are two different acts

questions.explanation: The sentence has merged two acts that a reader needs kept apart. Somebody wrote a report; somebody then told the committee what the report said. A report can be quoted directly, in which case the words belong to the document and the report's own author is the source. A claim can be attributed as something a person said, in which case the person is the source and their standing is what tells the reader how far to carry the words. Here the sentence uses the told construction, which requires an understood teller, and then supplies none, so the reader learns that a number exists and nothing at all about who is standing behind it. That is a different fault from an uncheckable number: the figure may be perfectly good, and the sentence still has removed the one thing that would let a reader weight it.
questions.hint: Ask who the understood subject of 'was told' is.

questions.topic: A source dropped between two of a paper's own reports
questions.learningObjective: judge what a follow-up loses when it reprints a sourced claim unsourced

stimulus.body: Earlier report, 4 March: The depot's staffing was cut by a third in 2024, according to a review the operator commissioned and published in full. Follow-up report, 2 April: The depot's staffing was cut by a third in 2024. The depot now asks the authority to review its safety arrangements.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: Two of a paper's own reports read: 'Earlier report, 4 March: The depot's staffing was cut by a third in 2024, according to a review the operator commissioned and published in full.' and 'Follow-up report, 2 April: The depot's staffing was cut by a third in 2024. The depot now asks the authority to review its safety arrangements.' What has the follow-up done?

options.text: Dropped the source, so a claim its own paper had evidenced is republished as a bare assertion
Shortened the sentence, so the follow-up is quicker to read than the first report was
options.misconception: measures the change in length, when the missing element is the source

options.text: Used the word now, which makes a 2024 figure sound as though it is current
options.misconception: fixes on a tense, when the change is the loss of attribution

options.text: Omitted the year, so a reader cannot tell when the cut of a third happened
options.misconception: misses that 2024 is printed, and the omission is of the source

questions.explanation: The first report hands a reader the whole apparatus of the claim: a review, commissioned by the operator, published in full, so that a reader who doubts the figure has somewhere to go. The second report keeps the number and drops all of it, and the sentence that remains is a statement the paper is making on its own authority about a document it has stopped pointing at. The damage is not that the claim has changed, since it has not; it is that a reader of the follow-up cannot tell the claim is second-hand, and a reader who has seen both reports will have noticed that the evidence went missing without a correction being issued. A follow-up that is shorter is a normal and good thing. A follow-up that is shorter because the source has been dropped turns a piece of reporting into an assertion.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader of the second report has that a reader of the first had.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A partisan body cited as if it were neutral
questions.learningObjective: weigh an attribution that hides the source's interest

stimulus.body: Spending on the river walk rose by 18 per cent last year, according to the county's riverside business forum, which the chamber of commerce funds. The chamber said the rise showed that the council had taken business concerns seriously. The council's own budget papers list 6 per cent.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report reads: 'Spending on the river walk rose by 18 per cent last year, according to the county's riverside business forum, which the chamber of commerce funds. The chamber said the rise showed that the council had taken business concerns seriously. The council's own budget papers list 6 per cent.' What does the sentence do with the source?

options.text: It gives the source more credit than a figure taken from budget papers would get
options.misconception: adds an evaluative comparison the report does not make between the two sources' standing

options.text: It lets the figure reach the reader through a body with a stake in the figure being large
It keeps the funding quiet so that the reader is not distracted from the number
options.misconception: supposes an intention to conceal, which the sentence discloses and the reader may weigh

options.text: It shows two different bodies disagreeing, which is itself a sign that the figure is contested
options.misconception: reads a difference in number as a dispute between bodies, when both may count different things

questions.explanation: The sentence is not wrong to report the forum's figure, and disclosure is often thought to be enough. But look at what the attribution does. According to introduces the number, and a reader takes the introducing source as the origin of the number, so a figure that originates in a body funded by the chamber of commerce arrives looking like an independent count of council spending. The only clause that touches the interest, which the chamber of commerce funds, comes after the number has been stated and is itself a relative clause the eye can pass over. Disclosure placed after a figure does not stop the figure from doing its work. The other three answers each misdescribe what the paragraph says: the report never ranks the two sources, and it never conceals the funding, and the last two numbers need not be a dispute at all since a body's survey and a set of budget papers can count different things.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader believes about the number before reaching the clause about funding.

questions.learningObjective: judge whether a report has met its duty to a person named in it

stimulus.body: The supplier Halden Freight has been paid 1.2 million pounds by the authority in three years without going out to tender, according to a register published on Tuesday. The authority's procurement officer said the contract was covered by an exemption. Halden Freight did not respond to three requests for comment.

questions.stem: A report reads: 'The supplier Halden Freight has been paid 1.2 million pounds by the authority in three years without going out to tender, according to a register published on Tuesday. The authority's procurement officer said the contract was covered by an exemption. Halden Freight did not respond to three requests for comment.' What does the report leave a reader without?

options.text: A reason for the exemption, since the officer gave the word without explaining the rule behind it
options.misconception: asks for a rule the report may properly leave to a later piece, when the fault is the missing side

options.text: The date of the register, which the sentence has already given as Tuesday
options.misconception: misses a date the sentence supplies and complains about a second one

options.text: Anything from the firm that is the subject of the figure, apart from its silence
Confirmation that the requests for comment were sent to the right people
options.misconception: demands a detail the report never claimed to have verified, and one no reader can check from it

questions.explanation: A report that names a firm and puts a four-figure sum against it has made an allegation with consequences, and the firm has been asked three times for a view. Silence is reportable, and the report has reported it correctly; what the report has not done is supply anything else, so the reader is left with a number attributed to a register, an exemption asserted by an officer and not explained, and a company that has said nothing. That combination is not neutral. It is a structure in which the two available accounts are the register and the officer, and the third party is present only as a gap. A reader is entitled to know not merely that a firm declined but that it was asked, which the sentence does supply, and to be able to see that it has had no chance to answer an allegation of this size. The other three answers chase facts the sentence supplies, asks for, or never promised.
questions.hint: Count the accounts a reader has and ask whether the named party is one of them.

questions.topic: A report that hears one side only
questions.learningObjective: identify the structural gap in a dispute written from a single account

stimulus.body: Residents of Brack Lane have complained for two years that the new footbridge is too steep, and a petition signed by 340 households asks for it to be rebuilt. The parish council said the gradient was built to the standard the highway authority requires and that a rebuild would cost 2.6 million pounds. The petition is due to be considered at the next meeting.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: Two documents read: 'Residents of Brack Lane have complained for two years that the new footbridge is too steep, and a petition signed by 340 households asks for it to be rebuilt. The parish council said the gradient was built to the standard the highway authority requires and that a rebuild would cost 2.6 million pounds. The petition is due to be considered at the next meeting.' The report quotes the council's reply. What has the report still not done?

options.text: Said how many of the 340 households live on Brack Lane, which is the real measure of support
options.misconception: asks for a figure that would be guesswork, since the petition says households and the road has a separate number of homes

options.text: Checked the cost of a rebuild against the council's budget, which would show whether 2.6 million is affordable
options.misconception: asks for a budget comparison the report may leave until the council publishes one

options.text: Named the highway authority's standard, so the reader can judge the council's defence
options.misconception: asks for the defence to be dismantled rather than for the report to be complete

options.text: Put the residents' own case in their words, since a signatory count is not a view

questions.explanation: The document gives the residents' position three times over: for two years, by way of a petition, and by number. It gives it three times over and never in their words. A report built this way is not even-handed, it is one-sided in a way a reader cannot see the seam of, because the two accounts sit in the same paragraph and read as a summary of a position rather than as the reporting of a dispute. The council has a version delivered in an attributed sentence; the residents have a grievance delivered in the report's own voice, which is the voice of a document summarising them. A reader can weigh cost against petition and find neither side audible. The three alternatives each ask for something a report may legitimately defer: a household-by-household breakdown of a petition, a budget comparison that depends on a figure the council controls, and the text of a standard that the council has already invoked and that the council, not the report, is best placed to produce.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the dispute is quoted and which is summarised.

questions.learningObjective: weigh a conclusion whose base is a single short period

stimulus.body: The number of late trains recorded on the Marlow branch rose in May, from 41 to 96. The operator said the increase was caused by a shortage of drivers recruited in March, and added that the line has never run so badly. A count taken over the twelve months to March records 610 late trains, an average of 51 a month.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report reads: 'The number of late trains recorded on the Marlow branch rose in May, from 41 to 96. The operator said the increase was caused by a shortage of drivers recruited in March, and added that the line has never run so badly. A count taken over the twelve months to March records 610 late trains, an average of 51 a month.' What is the strongest objection to the operator's second claim?

options.text: One month cannot support never, and the twelve months the report supplies cut the other way
The figure of 96 is a count for one month, so any comparison with another month is unstable
options.misconception: attacks the figure's comparability, which the report's own twelve-month total answers

options.text: A driver shortage is not the same thing as a signalling fault, so the cause may be misattributed
options.misconception: raises a rival cause the text does not raise, and the report offers no evidence for one

options.text: The line has run for decades, so a single month says little about the condition of the track
options.misconception: adds an appeal to length of history that the report's own figures make unnecessary

questions.explanation: The words are never run so badly and the base is one month. A universal claim about the history of a line cannot be established by a month's count, and the report does not leave the reader to speculate, because it supplies the twelve months to March: 610 late trains, an average of 51 a month, against a May figure of 96. options.misconception: reads the fall as a verdict, which is a question the report's own figures do not settle

options.text: That a large number of people stopped complaining, when the number fell from 118 to 47

options.misconception: misses that the first sentence carries no figures at all

The report's second sentence is where the actual movement is, and it is 118 to 47, a fall of 71 complaints across two six-month periods on a system that had only just opened. The size of the relative change is real, and it is still misleading standing on its own, because 47 is a small number of complaints in absolute terms and a reader who never saw the second sentence has been given a very different impression of the arithmetic. The other three answers either credit the sentence with a conclusion it does not draw, treat a missing condition as the fault when the missing numbers are the fault, or ask about a figure the sentence does not contain.

options.misconception: supplies a comparability fault the report does not commit and a reader cannot see

options.misconception: clears the rounding and blames the number, when the number and the claim are one sentence

options.text: Compared a total with a budget without saying the budget, so the comparison is loose
options.misconception: identifies a real omission that is not the fault, since the missing budget explains the word overspent

options.text: Written more than 400 million when the return says 412,660,000, so the figure is inconsistent

options.text: Rounded the figure in a direction that inflates the claim built on it

A report that rounded down to 412 million and wrote more than 400 million would be saying the same thing and would be telling the truth twice over.

The trust said 40 clinical posts were unaffected. The plan is subject to consultation with unions beginning in September.' What does the headline add?

Nothing, since the number 200 and the verb cut both appear in the body

options.misconception: supplies a counting rule, when the fault is that the comparison is unstated

options.text: The comparison the word highest is standing in for: a period, a set, and the number it beat
A quotation from an official, since records are usually established by the operator

options.text: A caveat, since a record is by nature provisional and may be revised
options.misconception: adds a general caution that does not address what the word highest leaves out

It is not enough for a report to have done the comparison privately; the claim is being made in a sentence that a reader cannot check, so the comparison has to be in the sentence or in a note attached to it. options.text: A comparison with other branches, so the branch can be judged against the rest

I have the minutes of the meeting where we were told it. I am happy to publish them.' A report prints: 'A councillor said the drainage had not been finished before the winter and that the council never checked on its promises.' What has the shortening done?

options.text: Cut twenty-four words down to eleven, which is what an editor is obliged to do to a quotation
options.misconception: measures the change in words, when what matters is what the shorter sentence now asserts

options.text: Left out which office the councillor holds, since a reader has no need of a title
options.misconception: invents a privacy rule where the report already names the council in its attribution

options.text: Omitted the minutes, because a document a speaker happens to hold needs no mention

stimulus.body: Tenant at the residents' meeting on 3 March: 'The water came into the ground-floor flat twice in February. Nobody from the housing office came.' Tenant at the meeting on 4 March: 'We did not know about the damp. The housing office never told us.' Report text: 'A tenant said the housing office was never told about the damp in her flat.'

questions.stem: A tenant said at one meeting: 'The water came into the ground-floor flat twice in February. Nobody from the housing office came.' At the next meeting she said: 'We did not know about the damp. The housing office never told us.' A report prints: 'A tenant said the housing office was never told about the damp in her flat.' What has the report produced?

options.text: A quotation shortened to fit a line, which is the ordinary reason for trimming
options.misconception: explains a routine editorial act when the trimmed version changes the claim

options.text: A report that has chosen one of two meetings and said nothing about it
options.misconception: finds a fault in the selection, which is not what the printed sentence misstates

options.text: A claim about who failed to inform, which is the very point in dispute
A tenant's account of her own flat, which no one else could contradict
options.misconception: treats a disputed matter as one only she can speak to, which is the opposite of the fault

questions.explanation: Follow the claim through both remarks. What the tenant said on 4 March is that the office did not tell her, which is a complaint that nobody informed her, and a reader is meant to understand that the office ought to have. The report has printed the housing office was never told, which is a different proposition: it says the office was not informed, and that is the question in dispute, because the office's account is that no damp was reported. The report has therefore taken a complaint and restated it as a finding against the party complained of, and it has done so by joining two sentences from two meetings and selecting the fragment that carries the claim. Note also what has gone: twice in February and nobody came, which are the two facts that would let a reader judge the complaint rather than accept it.

questions.topic: A condition dropped from a quotation

questions.stem: A spokesperson said: 'If the figures are confirmed by the audit, we will repay the overcharge to the households affected.' A report prints: 'A spokesperson said the firm would repay the overcharge to the households affected.' What has changed?

options.text: The subject has been named, so the report is more precise than the remark was
options.misconception: misses that the report has lost the audit clause while gaining a subject

options.text: The quotation has been shortened, which is allowed within quotation marks
options.misconception: clears the edit, when the words retained say something the speaker did not

options.text: The firm has been named, which a report may not do from an unnamed briefing
options.misconception: invents a restriction, since a firm named in the briefing is properly nameable

options.text: The undertaking's condition has gone, so what was conditional now reads as a promise

If the figures are confirmed by the audit is the part that makes the repayment contingent, and it is the whole of the speaker's position: a promise made in advance of the evidence that would trigger it. Delete it and the firm has undertaken to repay, which is a stronger statement about a company in dispute with the households in question, and a reader cannot tell from the printed sentence that anything was conditional. This is the commonest and most consequential of quotation faults, because a conditional is exactly the part a reader is entitled to be given. questions.topic: A correction that corrects nothing
questions.learningObjective: judge a notice that never states what was wrong

stimulus.body: CORRECTION: A report on 3 May said 96 late trains had run on the Marlow branch in May. Readers may find this figure surprising. The operator publishes its performance data at the end of each quarter and readers are referred to that data.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A notice reads: 'CORRECTION: A report on 3 May said 96 late trains had run on the Marlow branch in May. Readers may find this figure surprising. The operator publishes its performance data at the end of each quarter and readers are referred to that data.' What is wrong with the notice?

options.text: It repeats the wrong figure, so the error will keep circulating after the notice
options.misconception: condemns a repetition that is how a reader learns what changed

options.text: It never says what was wrong or what the right figure is, so nothing has been corrected
It refers readers elsewhere, so they must fetch the data to learn the position
options.misconception: objects to a pointer, which is standard practice once the error is actually stated

options.text: It uses the word surprising, which implies the figure was doubtful when it was not
options.misconception: attacks an adjective when the notice's failure is that it states no correct figure

questions.explanation: A correction does two things and must do both. It repeats what was published, so that a reader holding the earlier version can find the change, and it states the truth, so that a reader holding nothing can still get it. This notice does the first and omits the second entirely: readers are told that 96 appeared, told that they may find it surprising, and then referred to a quarterly release. Surprising is not an error statement, and a pointer is not a correction, so a reader who has seen only the notice has learned nothing except that the paper is aware of something. The number is still standing as the last word in the paper's own voice. The other three answers each find a feature that a well-run correction is built on: the repetition, the reference, and a plain description of the mistake are all correct practice here, and the failure is that the second half is missing.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who has not seen the original learns from this notice.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: What separates a retraction from a correction
questions.learningObjective: distinguish fixing a fact from withdrawing a claim
questions.stem: A piece has published a report that turned out to rest on a number the paper had obtained wrongly. What is the difference between correcting the number and retracting the report?

options.text: A correction is issued quietly; a retraction is announced at the top of the site
options.misconception: makes the difference one of prominence, when the difference is what is being withdrawn

options.text: A correction is about a fact and a retraction is about a source, since a report fails through its reporting
options.misconception: makes the difference one of subject matter, when it is one of how much of the report goes

options.text: A correction replaces the number; a retraction withdraws the report that was built on it
A correction is optional; a retraction is compulsory, because only a withdrawn report needs a notice
options.misconception: invents a compulsory rule, since both are the same instrument used to different depths

questions.explanation: The two notices differ in scope, not in ceremony. A correction says a particular statement was wrong and gives the version that is right, which leaves the rest of the report standing: if a piece said 480 late trains and the figure was 410, the piece is right about everything else. A retraction says the report itself should not have been published, which is the honest description when the number was load-bearing, and there is no correction to a report that should not have run. This is why a paper can print a correction and leave the headline alone, and why it cannot print a correction to a story it knows was wrong at the level of the claim. The other three answers each move the difference off scope, one to prominence, one to what the two notices are about, and one to whether a notice is compulsory at all; none of them decides whether a reader has been misled, which is the only question either notice exists to answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the number was doing in the argument, not where the figure appeared.

questions.topic: What a correction notice must carry
questions.learningObjective: select the content of an effective correction
questions.stem: Which of the following belongs in a correction notice?

options.misconception: turns a reader-facing notice into an internal post-mortem nobody can act on

options.text: A judgement of whether the error changed the argument of the piece

options.misconception: converts a notice into a personnel record, which is a different document entirely

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: An embargo broken by timing
questions.learningObjective: judge a report that is right about the fact and wrong about the time

stimulus.body: The league said on Monday that the result of Saturday's fixture would be released at noon. A report published at 09:40 on Monday said the home side had won two goals to nil, citing a statement from the club. The league said the result had been announced early in error by the club and asked for the accuracy of reports to be checked.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report reads: 'The league said on Monday that the result of Saturday's fixture would be released at noon. A report published at 09:40 on Monday said the home side had won two goals to nil, citing a statement from the club. The league said the result had been announced early in error by the club and asked for the accuracy of reports to be checked.' What is the fault?

options.text: Nothing in the fact; the report has broken a time the league had set
The report cited a club, which has an interest in the result and is not neutral
options.misconception: attacks the source where the only established fault is the hour of publication

options.text: The league asked for accuracy to be checked, so the score must be wrong as well
options.misconception: reads a complaint about timing as a verdict on the figure

options.text: A league fixture is not news, so nothing should have been reported on Monday
options.misconception: supplies a rule against reporting sport, which the report has not broken

questions.explanation: Two things are separable in this passage and the report has got one of them right. The score is not in dispute: the club announced it early in error, which is an admission that the information existed and was not meant to be out, not that the figure was false. What the report did was publish at 09:40 something that had been set for noon, and that is a breach of a stated time, which in sport means a person or a market who relied on the hour. A report that gets a fact right and a time wrong is still wrong, but the reader who is judging the piece needs to know which of the two has failed, and the league's own wording, an appeal for the accuracy of reports, obscures exactly that. The other three answers each go somewhere the text does not support: the club is a proper source for its own result, an appeal about accuracy is not a finding that the number is false, and no rule prevents a league result being reported at all.
questions.hint: Separate the figure from the hour and see which one is wrong.

options.misconception: supplies a preference, where the cost is a fixed delay before the reader has any fact

options.text: A reader must finish the quotation before learning who spoke or what has happened
The speaker's office, which a report should give in full before the words

options.misconception: raises a clarity worry, where the denial is plainly stated in the quotation itself

questions.topic: A caption that states an intention
questions.learningObjective: judge what a caption may claim beyond what the image shows

stimulus.body: IMAGE: A photograph taken at 07:10 outside a supermarket, the shutters down, a printed notice on the door, and about thirty people waiting in a line along the pavement. CAPTION: Shoppers wait in frustration as the owners prepare to close the store for good.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A photograph is described in the file as follows: 'A photograph taken at 07:10 outside a supermarket, the shutters down, a printed notice on the door, and about thirty people waiting in a line along the pavement.' The caption reads: 'Shoppers wait in frustration as the owners prepare to close the store for good.' What has the caption claimed?

options.text: That the people are shoppers, which the queue outside a supermarket supports
options.misconception: questions a word the description does not contradict and the fault is elsewhere

options.text: The hour, which a caption for a morning photograph ought not to carry
options.misconception: objects to useful detail while ignoring the assertion the caption makes

options.text: A future intention, which nothing in the described picture can establish
More than a caption should, since the sentence runs to two clauses
options.misconception: judges by length, when the fault is what the longer sentence asserts

questions.explanation: A caption's authority comes from the picture, and a picture carries one kind of information: what was in front of the camera at a stated time. The description gives an hour, a shuttered front, a notice and a line of about thirty people, and every one of those is visible. prepare to close the store for good is none of them: it is a statement about the owners' intention, about the future, and about permanence, and none of it is in the frame. The word frustration is a claim about a mental state, which is at least arguable from a queue of thirty people at 07:10; the intention is not arguable at all. A caption that goes beyond the frame is doing the report's work without the report's checking, and if the caption is wrong the picture cannot correct it, because a picture of people waiting has no opinion about why.
questions.hint: Ask which of the caption's words would still be true if the picture showed something else.

A line of poplar trees stands along the left bank. Two men are standing on the near towpath, one of them holding a stick. The water covers the lawn and reaches the base of the poplars.' options.misconception: fixes on one unproven word and passes the caption's claim about the water

options.misconception: objects to a causal gloss while leaving the positional claim alone

options.misconception: objects to vocabulary when the caption's problem is what it places where

The figures have to be traceable, because a number with no document and no named person behind it is a number the paper cannot stand behind when challenged, and the trace is also what lets a sub-editor check the piece. The claim has to follow from the figures, because this is where the commonest failure in a contested piece sits: the evidence establishes a size and the sentence reaches a conclusion the size cannot carry. options.misconception: attaches a sourcing fault to a line that is a plain narrative statement, not a quotation

options.misconception: demands a cause no one has given and no reporter can supply, and misses the ordering fault

questions.stem: A desk sets headlines in 30 characters including spaces. A submitted headline reads 'Rail strike halts all northern services' and is set as 'Strike halts services'. The story concerns a walkout on one operator's routes. What has the cut done?

options.text: Turned the sentence into a statement of fact, which is what a headline should be
options.misconception: invented a change of tense, when the submitted headline is present tense too

options.text: Widened the claim, since all northern services and rail have both been removed
Shortened the line to fit a slot, which every submitted headline must be cut to
options.misconception: explains a necessary act without asking what the act changed, which is the whole of the question

options.text: Left no network in the line, which is the word a reader most needs to see
options.misconception: picks the less consequential of the two deletions, when removing rail also widens the claim

questions.explanation: A cut to a character budget is not a summarisation if the words that go are the ones that bound the claim. The submitted line names a mode, a rail, a strike, and a limit, all northern services, and what remains is Strike halts services, which is the same sentence with every boundary removed. The story is about a walkout by drivers on one operator's routes between two named towns, and a reader of the set headline would take it as a statement about the system as a whole. The fault is therefore not that the desk did its job, which it must, but that the words chosen to go were the ones carrying scope rather than the ones carrying decoration. Note that the two deletions have the same effect: rail narrows the claim to a mode and all northern widens it to a region, and the cut removed both.
questions.hint: Ask which words bounded the original claim, and whether the story as reported is bounded at all.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: An opening that has to be rewritten
questions.learningObjective: say what an opening owes a reader and rewrite it
questions.stem: A draft report opens: 'Following a review that was commissioned in 2023 and reported in 2024, and after a period of consultation during which 1,900 responses were received, the authority has decided that the service will be restructured. The service currently carries 40,000 journeys a week, of which 3,100 are made by passengers over 65. A revised timetable will be published in October.' In three or four sentences, say what this opening has to do to be worth keeping, and rewrite it.

answer.exemplar: The opening has to do two things in its first line: say what has been decided, and say to whom it applies. As printed it does neither, because the decision arrives in the ninth line of the sentence that is supposed to be the lede, behind two participles and a subordinate clause about a review and a consultation. Everything the writer has put first, the commissioning year, the reporting year, the number of responses, is background a reader may want on the second day, and the first duty of an opening is to be about the thing. The rewrite carries the decision, the scale and the affected group, and pushes the consultation history down: 'The authority will restructure the bus service in October, cutting the number of weekly journeys on the network from 40,000. The change will affect the 3,100 weekly journeys currently made by passengers over 65.' A reader who stops after that has the news, the size and the group affected, and a good answer will keep those three and move the 1,900 and the two years below them rather than cut them.

questions.explanation: An opening earns its length by the order of what it puts first, and this one puts first the two things a report is supposed to bury. A participle chain of the kind printed here, Following a review that was commissioned in 2023 and reported in 2024, and after a period of consultation during which 1,900 responses were received, is grammatical and easy to write and very hard to read, because the reader must hold a nine-line subject in suspension before reaching a single verb that says anything. Test an opening by asking which words would be lost to a reader if only the first line were printed: here the answer is the decision itself, which is the one word group that cannot be lost. The rewrite has to keep the decision, the volume and the affected group in that order, and the consultation material may stay as long as it moves down.
questions.hint: Ask which words would be lost to a reader if only the first line of the opening were printed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A report's last line
questions.learningObjective: say what a report's ending owes a reader and rewrite the line
questions.stem: A report ends: 'The trust has been asked to say by Friday whether it will accept the offer. The trust has said it will consider the offer. The offer expires on Friday at 17:00.' In three or four sentences, say what this ending fails to tell a reader, and rewrite the last line.

answer.exemplar: The ending fails because it puts the clock last and never says what is at stake. Three sentences are spent restating a procedural position that the first of them already gave, the second adds only that the offer will be considered, which is what a body says when it has not decided, and the third, the expiry, arrives after the reader has run out of reason to stay. A closing line in a report is the one sentence a reader is most likely to remember and the one most likely to be quoted, so it has to carry the consequence rather than the diary. A version that works: 'The offer closes at 17:00 on Friday, and if the trust has not accepted it by then the trust's outpatients will be referred to the hospital eight miles away, an extra journey of about 40 minutes each way.' The rewrite has kept every fact in the original and given them an order, and the cost to the reader is the part a reader can actually use.

questions.explanation: A closing line is not a summary and it is not a diary. It is the sentence a reader carries out of the piece, and the test is whether a reader who read only the first and last lines of this report would be able to act. As printed, the last line is a time and the middle sentence is a non-answer, so a reader who reads nothing else learns that something expires on Friday and no more. The information the ending needs is present in the wider case, in the facts about the referral route and the extra journey, and a good answer will bring one concrete consequence forward rather than simply rearranging the three sentences already there. The rewriting task also has a discipline component: the numbers in the exemplar must be the numbers of the case being written about, and a good answer keeps the expiry and adds the stake.
questions.hint: Ask what changes for a patient if the offer is not accepted, and whether the last line says it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: One story cut independently three times
questions.learningObjective: trace what independent cutting can do to a report's support

stimulus.body: STORY FILE, printed in order. A reporter files 14 paragraphs containing 6 attributed quotations and a box of figures. A sub-editor cuts the filed report to 8 paragraphs, dropping 3 of the quotations, and leaves the figures box where it is. A second sub-editor cuts the 8 paragraphs to 5 for the print edition and keeps 2 of the quotations that survive. The website version is set from the original 14 filed paragraphs, without the second cut. No stage is checked against the other stages.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A flow is printed as follows: 'STORY FILE, printed in order. A reporter files 14 paragraphs containing 6 attributed quotations and a box of figures. A sub-editor cuts the filed report to 8 paragraphs, dropping 3 of the quotations, and leaves the figures box where it is. A second sub-editor cuts the 8 paragraphs to 5 for the print edition and keeps 2 of the quotations that survive. The website version is set from the original 14 filed paragraphs, without the second cut. No stage is checked against the other stages.' What does this arrangement make possible?

options.text: A single correction, since every version is cut from the same filed report
options.misconception: assumes a single check, when no stage is checked against the others

options.text: A dropped figures box in print, which the second cut makes the likely outcome
options.misconception: predicts a particular cut that the flow does not record as having happened

options.text: A claim that carries a supporting quotation in print and has lost it online
A website version longer than the print version, since it keeps all 14 paragraphs
options.misconception: reports what the flow states without answering what the arrangement makes possible

questions.explanation: The website version and the print version are not two cuts of one text; they are two cuts of the same filed text, taken at different places and never compared. The first sub-editor drops 3 of the 6 quotations, and the print version then keeps 2 of what is left, so a claim in the piece may stand in print with a quotation supporting it and stand online with none. A reader of one version has a piece that is better evidenced than the piece the other reader is holding, and neither paper nor reporter knows which reader has which. That is the cost of cutting independently, and it is not a cost that appears in either version: each looks complete on its own. The other three answers each describe something the flow does or does not state rather than what the arrangement permits, and one of them supplies a check that the flow explicitly says is absent.
questions.hint: Ask which version keeps the quotations, and whether anyone compares them.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: What an alias has to do
questions.learningObjective: select the requirements that make an alias usable
questions.stem: A report uses an alias for a source who is not named. Which three things must the report do?

options.text: Apply the alias everywhere, so the same source is not called two different things
Say why the source is not named, so a reader can weigh the account accordingly
Give as much as can be given without identifying them, so the account is not empty
Keep the alias out of the headline, since a headline travels further than the text
options.misconception: sets a rule about where an alias may appear, which is not what makes one workable

options.text: Use a first name only, so the source still reads to a reader as a person
options.misconception: confuses a courtesy with a protection, since a first name identifies in the way a surname does

options.text: Change the alias at a stated interval, so a reader cannot follow one thread across reports
options.misconception: recommends an inconsistency that would break the continuity an alias exists to protect

questions.explanation: An alias is a substitution, and it works only if it is used as one. The first requirement is consistency, because the moment a source is called one thing and then another within a piece, the first name attaches to the second and the protection is gone; that is the fault examined earlier in this unit. The second is disclosure of the reason, because an unnamed source is a standing invitation to a reader to assume the account is a plant, and the reader is better placed to judge the account when told that the source cannot be named, is not paid, or is not a witness. The third is detail without identification, because an account with the alias and nothing else is not evidence a reader can weigh, whereas an account that gives the source's position, their access to the facts and the limits of what they saw is usable. The other three proposals each weaken the substitution.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do with an account that carries a name that is not the name.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A quotation that arrives by two steps
questions.learningObjective: judge the weight of a claim reported at second hand

stimulus.body: The site was never inspected in 2023, the union's regional officer told members at a meeting in Keighley. The report has no record of who attended that meeting, and the union has not published what was said.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report writes: 'The site was never inspected in 2023, the union's regional officer told members at a meeting in Keighley.' The report has no record of who attended the meeting and the union has not published what was said. What is the problem for a reader?

options.text: The claim is about an inspection, which the reporter ought to have checked independently
options.misconception: demands an independent check when the fault is the two-step chain the sentence builds

options.text: A union officer is not a neutral source on a matter involving a site and its staffing
options.misconception: attacks the source's neutrality, which is a different objection from the chain of transmission

options.text: The meeting's town is named, so a reader can identify everyone who was present
options.misconception: turns a possible route to verification into a verification already achieved

options.text: The words arrive by two steps, and neither the meeting nor the remark can be checked

questions.explanation: Read the sentence as a piece of machinery rather than as a claim. What the report has is a remark; what it prints is that the remark was made, at a meeting, to members, and the claim itself is inside quotation marks that the report did not witness. Both links in that chain are unverifiable here, and neither is unusual in themselves: a union officer speaking at a members' meeting is a proper occasion and a proper speaker. What makes the sentence weak is that the report offers nothing else, and a reader holding it has a specific checkable claim, that the site was never inspected in 2023, resting entirely on a sentence it cannot see. The other three answers each raise something a reporter might rightly do or rightly judge, and none of them is the gap between what the sentence asserts and what can be established.
questions.hint: Count the steps between the officer's mouth and the reader's eye.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A first sentence that rests on the thing in doubt
questions.learningObjective: weigh a sentence against the material the report supplies against it

stimulus.body: The council said this week that it has inspected the Fenwick bridge four times since 2021 and that a survey found no defect requiring work. A report on the bridge published in 2021 recommended that the deck be inspected twice a year, and the council did not adopt that recommendation. The bridge carries 6,000 vehicles a week, and the authority has published no record of the four inspections.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A report reads: 'The council said this week that it has inspected the Fenwick bridge four times since 2021 and that a survey found no defect requiring work. A report on the bridge published in 2021 recommended that the deck be inspected twice a year, and the council did not adopt that recommendation. The bridge carries 6,000 vehicles a week, and the authority has published no record of the four inspections.' What is the strongest objection to the first sentence?

options.text: It states as established the one thing the report then supplies a source to doubt
The survey is not dated, so a reader cannot tell whether it predates the 2021 report
options.misconception: asks about a date the objection does not turn on, since the claim covers the whole period

options.text: The council said it, so the sentence is attributed and cannot properly be questioned
options.misconception: treats attribution as immunity, when attribution is what makes a sentence answerable

options.text: Six thousand vehicles a week is a large figure, so a finding of no defect is surprising
options.misconception: argues from the volume of traffic, which the objection does not need to make

questions.explanation: The sentence bundles two claims, and the report immediately supplies a doubt about one of them. The council said it has inspected the bridge four times since 2021, and the last clause of the report says the authority has published no record of the four inspections. The objection is not that the record would prove the inspections happened, since a record would be a record of the council's own making; it is that the report has printed, in its own voice and at its own length, the absence of any check on a claim it has led with, and has done so without noting that the sentence's two halves rest on very different footing. The survey finding and the count of inspections are also doing different work, since one is a result and one is an assertion about a process, and the sentence presents them as a single established fact. The other three answers each argue about a detail rather than about the load the sentence is carrying.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two claims in the first sentence the last clause of the report touches.
